notes.front: What is a complexity analysis, in one sentence?
notes.back: An analysis used to identify resource requirements and check whether the current management structure still fits the incident.
notes.explanation: Too few resources risks lives and property; too many risks unqualified staff working without proper supervision.
notes.example: Like a hospital checking whether its current staffing still fits a ward as patient numbers change overnight.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 13, SM-188

notes.front: What is Resource Typing, in one sentence?
notes.back: Defining and categorizing incident resources by capability, so responders get the right personnel and equipment.
notes.explanation: Ordering a resource by name alone can bring the wrong tool for the job; typing fixes what "right" means.
notes.example: Like ordering a specific van size for a delivery, rather than just asking for "a vehicle."
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: What does Capability mean in Resource Typing, in one sentence?
notes.back: The core capability for which a resource is most useful.
notes.explanation: It is the broadest of the four typing elements: which core capability the resource is most useful for.
notes.example: Like sorting tools by the job they're bought for, before even asking what kind of tool each one is.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: What does Category mean in Resource Typing, in one sentence?
notes.back: The function for which a resource is most useful, such as firefighting, law enforcement, or health and medical.
notes.explanation: Category narrows Capability down to a specific function, one step closer to naming the actual resource.
notes.example: Like sorting tools by trade (plumbing, electrical) after already sorting by the job they support.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: What does Kind mean in Resource Typing, in one sentence?
notes.back: A broad class of resource: personnel, teams, facilities, equipment, or supplies.
notes.explanation: Kind says what the resource physically is, separate from what job (Category) it does.
notes.example: Like knowing you need "a team," before knowing which kind of team.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: What does Type mean in Resource Typing, in one sentence?
notes.back: A resource's minimum capability to do its function, based on size, power or capacity, or on experience and qualifications.
notes.explanation: Type is the most specific typing element: it says how capable a given Kind of resource actually is.
notes.example: Like ordering "a Type 3 ambulance" instead of just "an ambulance," so you know its exact capability.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: What is the Resource Typing Library Tool (RTLT), in one sentence?
notes.back: FEMA's online catalogue of national resource typing definitions, position qualifications, and Position Task Books.
notes.explanation: It gives every jurisdiction one shared reference, so a "Type 3 Ambulance Ground Team" means the same thing everywhere.
notes.example: Like a national parts catalogue that lets any supplier order the exact same standard component.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 21, SM-197

notes.front: What is Incident typing, in one sentence?
notes.back: Categorizing incidents into five types by complexity, from Type 5 (least complex) to Type 1 (most complex).
notes.explanation: It supports decisions about resource requirements and which Incident Management Team level to order.
notes.example: Like a hospital's triage categories, but sized to the whole incident rather than one patient.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 24, SM-200

notes.front: What is an Incident Management Team (IMT), in one sentence?
notes.back: A rostered group of qualified personnel: an Incident Commander, Command and General Staff, and others in key incident command positions.
notes.explanation: An IMT is a ready-made team that can be ordered as a unit, rather than assembling qualified people one by one.
notes.example: Like calling in a whole pit crew at once, rather than hiring each mechanic separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: Does flexibility in incident command allow nonstandard organizational structures or position titles?
notes.back: No: flexibility is exercised only within the standard incident command structure and standard position titles.
notes.explanation: Flexibility scales the organization up or down; it never overrides Common Terminology.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 2, SM-175

notes.front: What three things is an incident command organizational structure based on?
notes.back: Size and complexity of the incident; the hazard environment; the incident planning process and objectives.
notes.explanation: The structure is not fixed in advance: it grows out of what the specific incident actually needs.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 3, SM-176

notes.front: What three rules govern how the incident command organization expands or contracts?
notes.back: Fill only positions needed for objectives; give each activated element a person in charge; keep an effective span of control.
notes.explanation: There are no hard-and-fast rules beyond these three, which is exactly what makes the structure flexible.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 5, SM-178

notes.front: Can a Unit be activated without its Section Chief being assigned?
notes.back: Yes: for example, the Situation Unit can be activated without a Planning Section Chief; the Incident Commander then supervises it.
notes.explanation: Many organizational elements can be activated in a Section without activating that Section's Chief.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 7, SM-180

notes.front: If staffing is short, should you combine incident command positions and invent a shortened or combined title?
notes.back: No: assign one person to supervise multiple units instead, using only standard titles.
notes.explanation: Nonstandard titles may be unrecognizable to assisting or cooperating personnel and can cause confusion.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 9, SM-182

notes.front: Which step of the incident resource management process is about working out what resources the incident needs?
notes.back: Identifying Requirements.
notes.explanation: The six steps run in this order, from working out the need to closing it back out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: Which step of the incident resource management process is about requesting and obtaining the resources identified?
notes.back: Ordering and Acquiring.
notes.explanation: The six steps run in this order, from working out the need to closing it back out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: Which step of the incident resource management process is about moving the resources to the incident?
notes.back: Mobilizing.
notes.explanation: The six steps run in this order, from working out the need to closing it back out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: Which step of the incident resource management process is about keeping an accurate picture of where resources are and what they're doing?
notes.back: Tracking and Reporting.
notes.explanation: The six steps run in this order, from working out the need to closing it back out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: Which step of the incident resource management process is about releasing resources that are no longer needed?
notes.back: Demobilizing.
notes.explanation: The six steps run in this order, from working out the need to closing it back out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: Which step of the incident resource management process is about paying for and replenishing what was used?
notes.back: Reimbursing and Restocking.
notes.explanation: The six steps run in this order, from working out the need to closing it back out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: What is one example of a predictable incident workload pattern from the Student Manual?
notes.back: Operations: the workload is immediate and often massive from the start.
notes.explanation: Recognising these patterns in advance helps managers anticipate staffing needs before they become urgent.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 12, SM-185

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about the safety of the community and responders?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about impacts to life, property and the economy?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about potential hazardous materials?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about weather and other environmental influences?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about the likelihood of cascading events?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about a potential crime scene, including terrorism?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about political sensitivity, external influences and media relations?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about the area involved and jurisdictional boundaries?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which complexity factor is about the availability of resources?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A complexity analysis weighs several such factors together; no single one decides the incident's complexity alone.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: Which resource Type is the most capable: Type 1 or Type 4?
notes.back: Type 1: resource types range from Type 1 (most capable) to Type 4 (least capable).
notes.explanation: This runs opposite to how many learners expect numbering to work, so it is worth fixing deliberately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 20, SM-195

notes.front: In the worked example, what defines a Type 3 Ambulance Ground Team?
notes.back: Category Emergency Medical Services, Kind Team: a crew of 2 (technician and operator), basic life support capability, transports 2 non-ambulatory patients.
notes.explanation: The example ties all four typing elements (Capability, Category, Kind, Type) together in one concrete resource.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: Why is ordering "a HazMat team" with no Type number risky?
notes.back: It could bring an inadequate resource: without a Type, capability, staffing and equipment are not specified.
notes.explanation: Kind alone names what the resource is, not whether it can actually do the job at hand.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 19, SM-194

notes.front: In which Type range do the vast majority of incidents fall?
notes.back: Type 3 to Type 5.
notes.explanation: Most incidents stay small and local; the largest, most complex Type 1 and 2 incidents are comparatively rare.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 25, SM-201

notes.front: What characterises a Type 5 incident?
notes.back: One or two single resources, up to six personnel; contained in the first operational period; no written Incident Action Plan.
notes.explanation: Type 5 is the smallest, simplest end of incident typing, such as a vehicle fire or a traffic stop.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 26, SM-202

notes.front: What characterises a Type 4 incident?
notes.back: Command/General Staff activated only if needed; several resources; one operational period; no written Incident Action Plan for non-hazmat incidents.
notes.explanation: Type 4 is a step up from Type 5: still one operational period, but with more resources and structure if needed.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 27, SM-203

notes.front: What characterises a Type 3 incident?
notes.back: Capabilities exceed initial response; some or all Command/General Staff and Division/Group/Unit positions activated; may run multiple periods, a written Incident Action Plan may be required.
notes.explanation: Type 3 is where a growing incident first outgrows a purely initial response and needs a fuller command structure.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 28, SM-204

notes.front: What characterises a Type 2 incident?
notes.back: Regional/national resources; most or all Command/General Staff filled; guidelines of ≤200 operations personnel per period, ≤500 total; written Incident Action Plan each period.
notes.explanation: Type 2 draws on resources beyond the local area, unlike the smaller types that stay within local capability.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 29, SM-205

notes.front: What characterises a Type 1 incident?
notes.back: National resources; all Command/General Staff and Branches activated; often >500 ops personnel per period, usually >1,000 total; may result in a disaster declaration.
notes.explanation: Type 1 is the largest, most complex incident type, the opposite end of the scale from Type 5.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 30, SM-206

notes.front: What level of Incident Management Team does Type 5 correspond to?
notes.back: Local Village and Township Level.
notes.explanation: IMT types correspond to incident type: the more complex the incident, the higher the team level ordered.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: What level of Incident Management Team does Type 4 correspond to?
notes.back: City, County, or Fire District Level.
notes.explanation: IMT types correspond to incident type: the more complex the incident, the higher the team level ordered.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: What level of Incident Management Team does Type 3 correspond to?
notes.back: State, Territory, Tribal, or Metropolitan Area Level.
notes.explanation: IMT types correspond to incident type: the more complex the incident, the higher the team level ordered.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: What level of Incident Management Team does Type 2 correspond to?
notes.back: National and State Level.
notes.explanation: IMT types correspond to incident type: the more complex the incident, the higher the team level ordered.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: What level of Incident Management Team does Type 1 correspond to?
notes.back: National and State Level (Type 1 Incident).
notes.explanation: IMT types correspond to incident type: the more complex the incident, the higher the team level ordered.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: What is the difference between a Strike Team, a Task Force, and a Single Resource?
notes.back: Strike Team: same kind and type. Task Force: mixed resources. Single Resource: one individual, crew, or item of equipment.
notes.explanation: All three share common communications and a designated leader, but differ in how uniform the resources inside them are.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 22, SM-197

notes.front: A vehicle fire near a chemical plant starts to threaten nearby storage tanks. What should the Incident Commander run to decide if the current staffing is still enough?
notes.back: A complexity analysis.
notes.explanation: It weighs factors like hazardous materials and cascading events to check whether the management structure still fits.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 13, SM-188

notes.front: "This resource exists to help deliver Public Health, Healthcare, and Emergency Medical Services" describes which typing element: Capability, Category, Kind, or Type?
notes.back: Capability: it names the core capability the resource is most useful for.
notes.explanation: Capability is the broadest of the four elements, tied to a core capability rather than a specific function.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: "This resource's function is emergency medical care" describes which typing element: Capability, Category, Kind, or Type?
notes.back: Category: it names the specific function the resource is most useful for.
notes.explanation: Category is narrower than Capability: it names a specific function, not a whole capability area.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: "This resource is a Team" describes which typing element: Capability, Category, Kind, or Type?
notes.back: Kind: it names the broad class the resource physically is.
notes.explanation: Kind says what the resource is (personnel, team, equipment) without yet saying how capable it is.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: "This resource is rated Type 3, with a crew of 2 and Basic Life Support capability" describes which typing element: Capability, Category, Kind, or Type?
notes.back: Type: it states the resource's minimum capability level.
notes.explanation: Type is the most specific element, defined by size, power, capacity, or experience and qualifications.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: A planner wants a nationally consistent definition for a "Type 2 Swiftwater Rescue Team" before ordering one. Where should they look?
notes.back: The Resource Typing Library Tool (RTLT).
notes.explanation: RTLT holds FEMA's national typing definitions, so "Type 2" means the same thing wherever it is ordered from.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 21, SM-197

notes.front: A regional emergency manager needs to decide what level of Incident Management Team to order for a growing wildfire. What should they use to help decide?
notes.back: Incident typing.
notes.explanation: Incident typing links an incident's complexity to decisions about resources and which IMT level to order.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 24, SM-200

notes.front: A state orders a rostered group with a qualified Incident Commander and full Command and General Staff to take over a large wildfire. What has it ordered?
notes.back: An Incident Management Team.
notes.explanation: An IMT is exactly this: a ready-made, qualified team rather than individually assembled staff.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: A supervisor invents the title "Ops-Log Coordinator" to cover both Operations and Logistics duties on a small incident. What has gone wrong?
notes.back: Flexibility was used to break Common Terminology: standard titles should never be combined or shortened.
notes.explanation: One person can hold two standard roles, but inventing a new, nonstandard title risks confusing other responders.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 2, SM-175

notes.front: Two incidents are the same size, but one involves a chemical spill and the other does not. Why might their command structures differ anyway?
notes.back: The hazard environment is one of the three things a command structure is based on, alongside size and objectives.
notes.explanation: Size alone does not decide structure: the specific hazards and the incident's objectives shape it too.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 3, SM-176

notes.front: An Incident Commander is tempted to activate every Section "just in case," even though only Operations is needed. Which expansion rule does this break?
notes.back: Fill only functions and positions necessary to achieve incident objectives.
notes.explanation: Activating unneeded elements adds supervision burden without adding useful capability.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 5, SM-178

notes.front: A small incident needs its Situation Unit active, but there is no one to serve as Planning Section Chief yet. Who supervises the Unit meanwhile?
notes.back: The Incident Commander.
notes.explanation: Units can be activated without their Section Chief; supervision then falls to the Incident Commander until one is assigned.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 7, SM-180

notes.front: Staffing is tight, so one person is asked to run both the Supply Unit and the Facilities Unit. What is the correct way to title this?
notes.back: Assign the person to both standard units under their existing standard titles, without inventing a combined title.
notes.explanation: The rule is not against one person doing two jobs; it is against inventing new, unrecognisable titles to describe it.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 9, SM-182

notes.front: A logistics officer has just released resources that finished their assignment and is now arranging to restock supplies. Which two steps of the resource management process is this?
notes.back: Demobilizing, then Reimbursing and Restocking.
notes.explanation: These are the last two steps in the six-step resource management process, closing out what was mobilized earlier.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 10, SM-183

notes.front: A structure fire draws national media attention because a well-known landmark is at risk. Which complexity factor does this reflect?
notes.back: Political sensitivity, external influences, and media relations.
notes.explanation: Complexity is not only about physical hazards; external attention can itself raise an incident's management complexity.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 14, SM-187

notes.front: A learner assumes a "Type 1" resource must be the smallest, since 1 sounds first and simplest. Why is this wrong?
notes.back: Type 1 is the most capable resource type; Types 2 to 4 have progressively less capability.
notes.explanation: Resource typing numbers run in the opposite direction to what many learners expect.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 20, SM-195

notes.front: Dispatch asks for "an ambulance resource, Team kind, capable of basic life support for two non-ambulatory patients with a 2-person crew." What resource Type is this describing?
notes.back: A Type 3 Ambulance Ground Team.
notes.explanation: The description matches the worked Type 3 Ambulance Ground Team example exactly: category, kind, capability and crew size.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: A dispatcher orders "a HazMat team" with no Type specified, and an under-equipped team arrives. What should have been ordered instead?
notes.back: A specific Type of HazMat team, such as "a Type 2 HazMat team."
notes.explanation: Kind alone does not guarantee adequate capability; adding a Type number specifies the minimum capability needed.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 19, SM-194

notes.front: A police traffic stop, handled by one officer within the hour, with no written plan: what incident Type is this?
notes.back: Type 5.
notes.explanation: One or two single resources, contained within the first operational period, matches the Type 5 definition exactly.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 26, SM-202

notes.front: An expanding wildfire now needs some Command and General Staff, plus Division Supervisors, and may run several operational periods. What incident Type is this?
notes.back: Type 3.
notes.explanation: Exceeding initial-response capability and adding Division/Group or Unit positions is the hallmark of a Type 3 incident.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 28, SM-204

notes.front: A disaster draws national resources, activates every Command and General Staff position and several Branches, with over 1,000 total personnel. What incident Type is this?
notes.back: Type 1.
notes.explanation: This is the most complex incident type: national resources, a full staff structure, and often a disaster declaration.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 30, SM-206

notes.front: A grass fire threatens a rural property. Two engines and a Task Force work the blaze for one operational period; no written IAP is drawn up, but a documented operational briefing is given. What incident Type is this?
notes.back: Type 4.
notes.explanation: Several resources, one operational period, Command/General Staff activated only if needed, and no written IAP for a non-hazmat incident matches the Type 4 definition.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 27, SM-203

notes.front: A flood response draws regional resources, fills most Command and General Staff positions, and stays under 500 total personnel with a written plan each period. What incident Type is this?
notes.back: Type 2.
notes.explanation: Regional or national resources with most Command and General Staff filled, but under the Type 1 personnel guidelines, points to Type 2.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 29, SM-205

notes.front: A state activates a rostered team qualified for national and state-level incidents to manage a Type 1 hurricane response. What IMT Type is this?
notes.back: Type 1.
notes.explanation: IMT Type 1 and Type 2 both correspond to the National and State level, so the incident's own Type is what tells them apart.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 31, SM-206

notes.front: Kind and Type both describe a resource. What is the actual difference between them?
notes.back: Kind says what a resource physically is (team, equipment); Type says how capable that Kind is, at a minimum standard.
notes.explanation: Learners often use the words interchangeably, but Kind is a category and Type is a graded capability level within it.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: Capability and Category can both sound like "what the resource is for." How do they differ?
notes.back: Capability is the broad core capability a resource serves; Category is the narrower function it performs within that.
notes.explanation: Capability groups resources at the level of the National Preparedness Goal's core capabilities; Category is one specific function inside it.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 17, SM-192

notes.front: A Strike Team and a Task Force are both groups of resources. What tells them apart?
notes.back: A Strike Team is resources of the same kind and type; a Task Force is a mix of different resources.
notes.explanation: Kind and Type are matched within a Strike Team; a Task Force is defined precisely by not sharing that constraint.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 6, Visual 22, SM-197
